lesson.title: One Connection, Many Requests: HTTP/1.1 Grows Up
lesson.summary: HTTP/1.1 refined the original protocol with persistent connections, a mandatory Host header, and chunked transfer encoding, becoming the version that carried the web for roughly two decades.
lesson.body:
HTTP did not arrive at the version shown throughout this chapter set all at once. HTTP/0.9 was a single line request with no headers and no status code at all. HTTP/1.0 added the headers and status codes used in every example so far, but it generally opened a fresh TCP connection for each single request. HTTP/1.1, standardized in RFC 2616 and later refined further, fixed enough of what made HTTP/1.0 inefficient that it became the version the web actually ran on for roughly the next two decades.

The biggest change was persistent connections by default. Under HTTP/1.0, fetching a page and then five images on it typically meant six separate TCP connections, each paying for its own three way handshake before a single HTTP byte could move. HTTP/1.1 keeps a single TCP connection open and reuses it for many requests and responses in sequence unless either side explicitly sends Connection: close, which turns that repeated handshake overhead from six times down to once.

HTTP/1.1 also made the Host header, introduced in the headers chapter, mandatory rather than optional. That single change is what made virtual hosting practical: one server with one IP address can answer for many completely different domains, because every HTTP/1.1 request is required to say which one it means.

Another addition was chunked transfer encoding. Under HTTP/1.0, a server generally had to know a response's full size in advance to send a correct Content-Length header. Chunked transfer encoding lets a server start sending a response in pieces before it knows the total size at all, which matters for dynamically generated content where the final length is not known until generation finishes.

HTTP/1.1 also technically allowed pipelining, sending several requests back to back on one connection without waiting for each response first. In practice this created a real problem: responses still had to come back in the same order the requests were sent, so one slow response blocked every response queued behind it on that connection, a problem generally called head of line blocking. Because of that, browsers largely avoided true pipelining and instead worked around the limitation by opening several parallel persistent connections to the same server, trading some of the efficiency gained from persistent connections for the ability to make progress on more than one request at a time. That specific limitation, one ordered stream of responses per connection, is precisely what later versions of HTTP were designed to address, though that is a story for a different chapter.
